explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. God tells Jacob, “Build an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.” Esau is Jacob's brother. So the order is simple: get up, go to Bethel, and build the altar. Nobody needs a blueprint for that one.

No wall in this verse, friend. God's words to Jacob are “Arise, go up to Bethel, and settle there.” The one thing He asks him to build is an altar to the God who appeared to him when he fled from his brother Esau. Jacob's wall-building days are not part of this instruction.

I get the thought, but a storehouse isn't what God asks for. He says, “Build an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.” Esau is Jacob's brother. This build isn't for storing anything. It's an altar to God.

Right on the money, friend. Jacob tells his household and all who were with him, “Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you.” That comes before anything else on his list. If you're headed to worship the one God, you drop the other gods at the door.

Nobody's counting sheep here, friend. Jacob tells his household and all who were with him, “Get rid of the foreign gods that are among you.” He's about to build an altar to God at Bethel (Genesis 35:3), so the first thing off the list is the stuff that doesn't belong. It's like clearing the counter before a big bake.

Ditch the tents? Then we're all standing in a field with nowhere to put the family, friend. That's not the plan. Jacob tells his household and all who were with him to get rid of “…the foreign gods that are among you.” Tents can come along to Bethel. The other gods can't.

Yes, friend. Jacob says, “Purify yourselves and change your garments.” Then he says they will go to Bethel, where he will build an altar to God. Whenever I put on a clean apron, I stand up a little straighter myself.
No haircuts on this list, friend. Jacob's words are, “Purify yourselves and change your garments.” So the other instruction is about clothes. Heads never come up.

Jacob doesn't give them a fasting plan, friend. What he says is, “Purify yourselves and change your garments.” There's no number of days in his words at all. The second instruction is simply a change of clothes.

That's it, friend! The household hands Jacob “…all their foreign gods and all their earrings…” (Genesis 35:4). Picture him standing there with his arms getting fuller and fuller. Then he buries the whole pile under the oak near Shechem, and they're ready to head for Bethel.

Sandals are a good guess, friend, but that's not the word in this verse. The household hands Jacob “…all their foreign gods and all their earrings…” Earrings is your blank. Then Jacob buries the whole pile under the oak near Shechem.

Staffs, friend? I can see why you'd reach for that one, but it's not in this verse. The household gives Jacob “…all their foreign gods and all their earrings…” Earrings is the blank. Then Jacob buries the lot under the oak near Shechem. I once stamped a whole batch before I checked the recipe, so I get it.
True, friend. The text says, “…Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem.” The "them" is the foreign gods and the earrings the household had just handed over. So both of them go under that oak.

This one is actually true. The text says, “…Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem.” That means the foreign gods and the earrings were buried, not carried along. So the whole pile stays in the ground at Shechem.
Yes, friend. The text says, “…a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities…” It came from God Himself, and it fell on the cities around them. I think that was good news for Jacob's sons.

A storm is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word here. The verse says, “…a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities, so that they did not pursue Jacob’s sons.” It came from God, and it fell on the cities around them. That's why nobody chased Jacob's family.

Famine isn't what hit those cities. The verse says, “…a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities…” So the cities were struck with terror as Jacob's family set out. Nobody's pantry is mentioned here.

It's the other way around, friend. The text says the terror from God fell over the surrounding cities “…so that they did not pursue Jacob’s sons.” So the cities did not chase them. That makes this one False.

False is right, friend. The terror from God fell over the surrounding cities “…so that they did not pursue Jacob’s sons.” So the cities do not chase them. The statement says they did, and that's why it's False.
That's the name, friend. The verse says, “There Jacob built an altar, and he called that place El-bethel…” That's the place Luz, which is also called Bethel. Same ground, one more name for it.

Beersheba is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the name in this verse. The text says, “There Jacob built an altar, and he called that place El-bethel…” He's in Luz, which is also called Bethel. The altar goes up there, and El-bethel is the name he gives the place.

Peniel does belong to Jacob's story, friend, just not this part. He named that place after wrestling with God (Genesis 32:30). Here at the altar, the verse says he “…called that place El-bethel…” Different spot, different name.

explanations.answer: God revealed Himself to him there as he fled
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says he named it El-bethel “…because it was there that God had revealed Himself to Jacob as he fled from his brother.” So the name remembers what God did at that spot. Jacob's back where it happened.

explanations.answer: He dug a deep well there years before
explanations.explanation: No well in this verse, friend. The reason the text gives is that “…it was there that God had revealed Himself to Jacob as he fled from his brother.” Jacob names the place for what God did. Digging doesn't come into it.

explanations.answer: He bought a piece of land there before
explanations.explanation: Land deals don't come up here, friend. The text gives the reason straight out: “…it was there that God had revealed Himself to Jacob as he fled from his brother.” That's why the altar's place gets its name. It has nothing to do with a purchase.
That's the name, friend. God says, “Instead, your name will be Israel.” And then the verse adds, “So God named him Israel.” Jacob now has a new name straight from God.
Ephraim is a name from this family, but it's not Jacob's new one. Ephraim is the name Joseph gave his second son (Genesis 41:52). God tells Jacob, “Instead, your name will be Israel.”
Reuel isn't the name God gives here, friend. God says to Jacob, “Instead, your name will be Israel.” The verse then says, “So God named him Israel.” That's the new name, and it's settled.
Yes, friend. God says, “A nation—even a company of nations—shall come from you, and kings shall descend from you.” That's a big promise to give a man. Kings are part of it.

Prophets are a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word God uses. He says, “A nation—even a company of nations—shall come from you, and kings shall descend from you.” The word in the verse is kings. That's a whole lot of future to hand one man in one breath.

Priests would be a good guess, friend, but God doesn't say that here. His words are, “A nation—even a company of nations—shall come from you, and kings shall descend from you.” He starts with a nation, stretches it to a company of nations, then adds kings. That promise gets bigger with every phrase.

Right, friend. God says, “The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you…” Abraham is Isaac's father (Genesis 25:19). So God names both of them as the ones He gave the land to, and says He will give it to Jacob and to his descendants after him.

Noah is a great name, friend, but he's not in this verse. God says, “The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you…” The name in that line is Abraham, with Isaac right behind him. Then God says the land is for Jacob and his descendants.

Lot's not on the guest list for this one, friend. God says, “The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you…” The blank is Abraham, and Isaac comes right after him. Then God turns to Jacob: the land is for him, and for his descendants after him.

Yes, friend. The text says, “…Jacob set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him—a stone marker—…” and then he pours a drink offering on it and anoints it with oil. So the answer is a stone pillar. I mark my spots with cookie stamps, so a stone marker is a step up.

The text doesn't mention a tent here, friend. It says Jacob “…set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him—a stone marker…” So what stands at the spot is a stone marker. No poles, no canvas.
A gate isn't what Jacob sets up. The verse says he “…set up a pillar in the place where God had spoken with him—a stone marker…” That's stone, friend, not wood. It's a marker for the spot.

True, friend. The text says Jacob “…poured out a drink offering on it and anointed it with oil.” The "it" is the stone pillar he just set up where God had spoken with him. So the drink offering goes on the pillar, and the oil follows.

That one is true, friend. The text says Jacob set up the pillar, “…and he poured out a drink offering on it and anointed it with oil.” So the drink offering really does go on the pillar. The oil comes right after.

That's it, friend. The midwife tells Rachel, “Do not be afraid, for you are having another son.” Rachel is in severe labor, so those words land in a hard moment. I think this is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: The worst part is over now
explanations.explanation: That isn't what the midwife says, friend. Her words are, “Do not be afraid, for you are having another son.” Her reason is the baby, and it's a son. The text doesn't say anything about the worst being over.
Jacob isn't mentioned in the midwife's words, friend. She says, “Do not be afraid, for you are having another son.” That's her whole reason. The text doesn't say where Jacob is standing.
Yes, friend. The verse says Rachel named him Ben-oni, “But his father called him Benjamin.” So the boy ends up with the name his father gave him. Verse 24 lists Joseph and Benjamin as Rachel's sons.
Joseph is already Rachel's son, friend. Verse 24 says, “The sons of Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.” This new baby is the other one. His father called him Benjamin.
Reuben isn't Rachel's son, friend. Verse 23 says he was Leah's firstborn, “…Reuben the firstborn of Jacob…” The baby here is Rachel's, and “…his father called him Benjamin.”
True, friend. The verse says Rachel “…was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).” So the text itself says those are the same place. One road, two names.

That one is actually true, friend. The text says Rachel “…was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).” The words “that is” tell us they're the same place. Ephrath and Bethlehem are one and the same.
It's the other way around, friend. The text says, “…Israel heard about it.” So he did hear. The text doesn't say what he did next.
False is right, friend. After Reuben's sin, the verse says, “…and Israel heard about it.” Israel is Jacob's new name. So the news did reach him.

That's him, friend. The verse says, “Jacob returned to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had stayed.” So Jacob comes back to his father Isaac at Mamre. Hebron is the other name for Kiriath-arba.

Laban is Jacob's uncle, his mother's brother (Genesis 29:10), but he's not who Jacob returns to here. The text says, “Jacob returned to his father Isaac at Mamre…” So it's Isaac at Mamre, near Hebron.

Ishmael isn't in this verse, friend. He was Abraham's son (Genesis 16:15). The text says, “Jacob returned to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron)…” So Jacob goes back to his own father.
That's right, friend. The verse says, “And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.” Both of Isaac's sons were there for it. It's a quiet and heavy moment, and the two brothers stand together.
Reuben isn't named at Isaac's burial, friend. The verse says, “And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.” Isaac's own sons did it. Reuben is Jacob's firstborn, not Isaac's son.
Joseph isn't named here, friend. The text says, “And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.” Those are Isaac's two sons, Esau and Jacob. Joseph is Jacob's son, so he's not who the verse names.
